group.title: Academic writing 2
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Among other things.
examples: The report examines, {inter alia}, housing and transport.
wrong: The study covers, inter alia, only one single topic and nothing else.

words.meaning: And other authors; used when citing a work with several writers.
examples: Smith {et al.} found a similar effect in 2019.
wrong: The paper by Smith et al. was written by Smith entirely alone.

words.meaning: With the necessary small changes made.
examples: The same rules apply, {mutatis mutandis}, to part-time staff.
wrong: The rule applies mutatis mutandis, with no adjustment whatsoever.

words.meaning: If all other factors stay the same.
examples: {Ceteris paribus}, higher prices reduce demand.
wrong: Ceteris paribus means we change every factor at once.

words.meaning: Until now or until the time mentioned.
examples: The study reveals a {hitherto} unknown species.
wrong: The hitherto unknown fact had been famous for centuries.

words.meaning: From the very beginning.
examples: The contract was declared void {ab initio}, as if it had never existed.
wrong: The plan was flawed ab initio, though it only went wrong at the very end.

words.meaning: In that place, thing or fact.
examples: The plan is cheap; {therein} lies its appeal.
wrong: The box was empty, and the gift lay therein.

words.meaning: An extra section added at the end of a book or document.
examples: An {addendum} at the end lists the new figures.
wrong: The addendum was the original opening page, written before anything else.

words.meaning: To the extent that.
examples: The model is useful {insofar as} its data are reliable.
wrong: The model is reliable insofar as its data are completely unreliable.

words.meaning: Because, or to the extent that.
examples: The trial was a success {inasmuch as} no patient was harmed.
wrong: The trial succeeded inasmuch as every patient was harmed.

words.meaning: For an even stronger reason.
examples: If adults struggle with the test, then {a fortiori} children will.
wrong: If children find it easy, then a fortiori adults will find it impossible.

words.meaning: Based on a first look, before closer examination.
examples: There is {prima facie} evidence of a link.
wrong: After years of detailed study, the prima facie view finally formed.

words.meaning: A large collection of written or spoken texts used for study.
examples: The analysis draws on a {corpus} of ten million words.
wrong: The corpus contained just one sentence.

words.meaning: A careful explanation or interpretation of a text.
examples: Her {exegesis} of the poem filled forty pages.
wrong: His exegesis left the text completely unexplained.

words.meaning: To define an idea so that it can be measured in research.
examples: We {operationalized} stress as heart rate during the task.
wrong: They operationalized the idea by keeping it vague and unmeasurable.

words.meaning: To question an idea that people usually accept.
examples: The essay {problematizes} the notion of progress.
wrong: She problematized the theory by accepting it without question.

words.meaning: To give something the most attention or importance.
examples: The book {foregrounds} the voices of workers.
wrong: The study foregrounds gender by never mentioning it.

words.meaning: To examine an idea critically and in depth.
examples: The course {interrogates} common ideas about success.
wrong: The essay interrogates the concept by simply repeating it.

words.meaning: To give something as evidence or proof.
examples: The author {adduces} several studies to support the claim.
wrong: She adduced no evidence, citing ten strong sources.

words.meaning: To set the exact limits of something.
examples: The first chapter {delimits} the scope of the study.
wrong: The paper delimits its scope by including every possible topic.

words.meaning: To place something in its wider setting so it can be understood.
examples: The guide {contextualizes} each painting within its period.
wrong: He contextualized the quote by removing all background.

words.meaning: The study of how history has been written and interpreted.
examples: Her course on the {historiography} of the war compares a century of accounts.
wrong: Historiography is the digging up of old coins in a field.

words.meaning: A classification of things according to their types.
examples: She developed a {typology} of urban neighborhoods.
wrong: The typology ignored every type and category.

words.meaning: A gap or missing part, especially in knowledge or a text.
examples: The study fills a {lacuna} in the research on sleep.
wrong: The lacuna was the most complete part of the manuscript.

words.meaning: Something that is needed or wanted.
examples: Clear data is the main {desideratum} for any new policy.
wrong: The desideratum was something nobody wanted or needed.

words.meaning: A long, serious piece of writing on one subject.
examples: He wrote a {treatise} on political economy.
wrong: The treatise was a short joke on a postcard.

words.meaning: A mistake in a printed text, or a note listing its correction.
examples: The journal printed an {erratum} correcting the table.
wrong: The erratum praised the article for having no mistakes at all.

words.meaning: A collection of detailed information on a subject, in one book.
examples: The {compendium} lists every known species of fern.
wrong: The compendium included just a single item.

words.meaning: To check results by using several methods or sources.
examples: We {triangulated} survey data with interviews.
wrong: They triangulated the result by relying on one source only.

words.meaning: The quality of a claim that could be shown false by a test.
examples: A good scientific theory needs {falsifiability}.
wrong: Its falsifiability meant no test could ever prove it wrong.

words.meaning: Very important and influential for later work.
examples: Her {seminal} paper changed the field.
wrong: The seminal study had no influence on anyone.

words.meaning: Found in many places throughout a text, used in references.
examples: The theme of exile appears {passim} in her letters.
wrong: The word appears passim, just once on a single page.

words.meaning: That is to say; namely.
examples: Two issues remain, {to wit}, cost and timing.
wrong: Two issues remain, to wit, nothing at all.

words.meaning: The duty or responsibility to do or prove something.
examples: The {onus} is on the researcher to show the effect is real.
wrong: The onus was on her, so she had no responsibility at all.

words.meaning: An example that clearly shows what is being said.
examples: Small towns are dying; this village is a {case in point}.
wrong: Her success was a case in point that disproved the claim.

words.meaning: To make an idea seem more likely to be true.
examples: The new findings {lend credence to} the theory.
wrong: The evidence lent credence to the claim by disproving it.

words.meaning: In the role or character of; considered as.
examples: Art {qua} art needs no further purpose.
wrong: He spoke qua chairman, though he held no position on the board at all.

words.meaning: The ability of a study to be repeated with the same results.
examples: The {replicability} of the experiment has been questioned.
wrong: Its replicability meant no one could repeat the result.

words.meaning: To mix up the effects of factors so a result is unclear.
examples: Age may {confound} the link between income and health.
wrong: The variable confounded the result by making it perfectly clear.

words.meaning: An organized mental or written framework for understanding information.
examples: Readers use a {schema} of a restaurant visit to follow the story.
wrong: The schema was a random heap of ideas with no structure.
